summary: Adds a mechanism to the Atom Syndication Format that lets publishers explicitly mark entries that have been removed from a feed. Without it, readers cannot tell a deleted entry from one that simply stopped appearing. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: If a newspaper takes back a story, it should print a note saying so. This memo gives news feeds a way to say this story was removed.

questions: how to mark deleted entries in an atom feed
how do feed readers know an entry was removed
what is the atom deleted-entry element
how to mark an entry as deleted in an atom feed
subtitle: A tombstone element that lets an Atom feed say an entry has been removed.

tldr.problem: In the base Atom format, once a reader has received an entry, there is no way to learn that the publisher later removed it from the feed.
tldr.mechanism: The at:deleted-entry element names the removed entry by its atom:id in a ref attribute and gives the removal time in a when attribute. It can sit inside a feed or stand alone as a Deleted Entry Document.
tldr.outcome: Readers can update caches and displays, but the signal is advisory: processors may ignore it, and it can be spoofed unless the feed's origin is verified.

today: RFC 6721 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the Atom deleted-entry element.

sections.title: The Problem of Vanished Entries
sections.content:
Atom (RFC 4287) is an XML format for lists of related items called feeds, made of entries. Its main use is syndicating Web content such as weblogs and news headlines.

If a publisher removes an entry that a consumer has already received and, say, put in a local cache, base Atom gives the consumer no way to find out. This RFC adds a way for publishers of feed and entry documents to explicitly identify removed entries, so consumers can adjust things such as their caches and user interfaces.
sections.eli5: Imagine a friend sends you notes, then throws one away. You still have your copy and do not know it was thrown away. This adds a note that says that one was thrown away.

sections.title: The at:deleted-entry Element
sections.content:
The element lives in the namespace http://purl.org/atompub/tombstones/1.0, written with the prefix at. It has two required attributes. ref MUST hold the atom:id of the removed entry. when MUST hold an RFC 3339 date-time for the instant of removal, with an uppercase T between date and time and an uppercase Z if there is no numeric offset.

Optional children are one at:by (a person construct naming who removed it), one at:comment (a text construct explaining why), any number of atom:link elements, one atom:source and any foreign elements. A feed MAY hold any number of these elements but MUST NOT hold two with the same ref and when.

The atom:source element lets an aggregator keep track of the feed an entry came from. It MUST be present when the element appears in a feed other than its source feed, or when an element that has a source feed is used in a Deleted Entry Document.
sections.eli5: The note names which story was removed and when. It can also say who removed it and why, like a sticky note saying removed because it was spam.

sections.title: Deletion, Republishing and Advisory Nature
sections.content:
A feed may contain both an atom:entry and an at:deleted-entry with the same id. The processor compares the when value with the entry's atom:updated value to decide which is current.

  • If when is equal to or more recent than atom:updated, the entry was published and then removed, and processors SHOULD ignore the older entry.
  • If when is older, the entry was republished after an earlier removal, and processors SHOULD ignore the older deleted-entry element.

The element is advisory only. Its presence does not guarantee the entry is gone, and an aggregator that already processed the entry may pay it no attention. Unknown foreign markup inside it MUST NOT cause processing to stop or an error to be signaled. Internationalized identifiers, xml:base and xml:lang work as they do in Atom.
sections.eli5: If the removal note is newer than the story, the story is gone. If the story was posted again after the note, the story is back. And readers do not have to listen to the note.

sections.title: Deleted Entry Documents
sections.content: A Deleted Entry Document holds exactly one at:deleted-entry element outside any feed, with that element as its root. It is serialized as XML 1.0, identified by the media type application/atomdeleted+xml, and MUST be well-formed. The RFC defines no DTD, so such documents need not be valid in the XML sense.
sections.eli5: Instead of putting the note inside the newsletter, you can send the note by itself as its own little page.

sections.title: Signatures and Encryption
sections.content:
An at:deleted-entry MAY carry an enveloped XML signature. Processors MUST NOT reject it just because they cannot verify it. Processors that do verify MUST support exclusive XML canonicalization and MUST be able to verify RSA signatures, and Atom documents SHOULD NOT use MACs for signatures. Because an aggregator may add an atom:source and break a signature, publishers of individually signed elements should strongly consider adding it before signing.

The root of a Deleted Entry Document MAY be encrypted with XML Encryption, and processors that decrypt MUST support AES-128 in CBC mode. Since encryption does not protect integrity, they SHOULD check a signature hash or an in-document hash. When both are used, it is generally best to sign first and then encrypt.
sections.eli5: The note can be signed like a letter with your handwriting, or locked in a box so only the right person can read it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with base Atom, an attacker can publish entries or deleted-entry elements reusing other feeds' atom:id values to trick an application into thinking an entry was removed or added. Processors are advised to ignore deleted-entry elements that refer to entries that have not previously appeared in the containing feed, and to verify the origin of the feed.

If a deleted-entry is signed with a different key than the entry it refers to, or an unsigned one deletes a signed entry, that can indicate spoofing, and processors must take steps to verify it.
sections.eli5: Someone could forge a note saying a real story was removed. So check that the note really came from the right newspaper.
